Matzot
maht-SOHT
noun / Hebrew term
Hebrew matstsot (plural of matstsah, unleavened bread or flat bread; root matsats, possibly related to pressing or extracting, or to pressing out the moisture). The term designates bread baked without leaven or yeast — the flat, crackerlike bread eaten during the seven days of the Passover season in obedience to Exodus 12:15–20 and 13:3–10. The Greek rendering is azumos (unleavened), from which Luke 22:1 refers to the “Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called the Passover.” The leaven-free character of matzot carries an intentional symbolic weight in Scripture: leaven is consistently used as a type of sin, corruption, and the old nature that is to be purged.

Biblical Definition

Matzot is the unleavened bread prescribed for the seven-day Passover season beginning the evening of Nisan 14/15 (Exod 12:15–20; Lev 23:5–8; Deut 16:3), eaten in haste by Israel at the Exodus and thereafter as an annual covenant-memorial rehearsal. The command is absolute: “Unleavened bread shall be eaten seven days; and there shall no leavened bread be seen with thee, neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters.” (Exod 13:7). The unleavened bread carried a double symbolism: it memorialized the speed of the Exodus (there was no time to let bread rise, Exod 12:39) and it enacted the holiness required of those in covenant with the holy God (leaven as type of sin and corruption must be purged from the household). Paul gives the apostolic application in 1 Corinthians 5:7–8: “Christ our Passover also has been sacrificed. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” The purging of physical leaven from Israel's households prefigured the purging of moral leaven from the Christian community. The Lord's Supper itself uses unleavened bread — the matzot of the Passover seder — as the bread Christ broke when He said “this is my body” (Luke 22:1, 7–20). Every matzot cracker in the Supper carries the typological weight of the Passover season's call to purity and the Exodus's call to urgent, delivered haste.

Webster 1828 Definition

Matzot (matstsot) is the unleavened flat bread prescribed for the Passover season in Exodus 12–13 and Leviticus 23 as a memorial of the Exodus haste and a type of the purging of sin from the covenant community — fulfilled in the New Testament's call to put away the leaven of malice and wickedness (1 Cor 5:7–8).

MATZOT. Hebrew matstsot (pl. of matstsah): unleavened flat bread; the bread prescribed for the seven-day Passover season (Nisan 15–21) in Exodus 12:15–20; 13:3–10; Leviticus 23:6–8; eaten by Israel at the Exodus in haste (no time for rising) and thereafter annually as a memorial of the deliverance.

2. The leaven-purging command: no leaven was to be found in any Israelite dwelling during the seven days (Exod 12:15; 13:7); severe covenant sanction for violation (Exod 12:15: “that person shall be cut off from Israel”). The household search and removal of leaven was a physical enacted ritual of covenant holiness.

3. Typological meaning: leaven as the type of sin's pervasive influence (Matt 16:6: “beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees”; 1 Cor 5:6–7: “a little leaven leavens the whole lump”). Matzot, by its absence of leaven, is the type of the holy community purged of the old corrupting nature.

4. New Testament application (1 Cor 5:7–8): “Christ our Passover also has been sacrificed. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” The Passover sacrifice being accomplished, the seven-day holiness the feast demanded is now the permanent character of the Christian community.

5. The Lord's Supper connection: Jesus broke bread at the Passover seder (Luke 22:7–20) — the bread He took was matzot, the Passover unleavened bread. Every observance of the Lord's Supper with unleavened bread carries this typological depth: the bread of haste and deliverance, now the body broken for our sins.

Key Scripture

Exod 12:15 — "Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; even the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses: for whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel."

Exod 13:7 — "Unleavened bread shall be eaten seven days; and there shall no leavened bread be seen with thee, neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters."

1 Cor 5:7 — "Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us:"

1 Cor 5:8 — "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."

Modern Corruption

Matzot has been evacuated of its typological significance in most evangelical practice: the Lord's Supper is often celebrated with leavened bread, and the Passover-season call to communal holiness (“purge out the old leaven”) is treated as Jewish ritual rather than as the New Testament's own model for church discipline and regenerate community life.

expand to see more

The widespread evangelical use of leavened bread in the Lord's Supper is not a salvation-level issue, but it quietly severs the typological connection that Paul explicitly draws in 1 Corinthians 5:7–8. When Paul says “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us celebrate the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth,” he is applying the Passover matzot-purge to the church's practice of removing the leavened sinner from its midst (1 Cor 5:1–6). The physical type (unleavened bread at Passover) and the apostolic application (purge out the leavened man; celebrate with sincerity and truth) are a connected argument. Recovering matzot's typological weight means recovering the church discipline imperative that Paul draws from it.

The historical-critical dismissal of the matzot regulations as late Priestly legislation imposed on an older nomadic shepherd festival destroys the typological intentionality the New Testament assumes. If the unleavened bread requirement is a Second Temple-era addition rather than Mosaic law, Paul's typological application in 1 Corinthians 5 loses its grounding: how can the leaven-purge of Exodus 12 be a type of the church's discipline if Exodus 12 was itself only composed in the post-exilic period? The Reformed answer is that the Mosaic authenticity of the Passover legislation is the foundation of Paul's typological argument — deny the former and the latter collapses.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Matzot roots in the Exodus night's urgent departure (no time for rising bread, Exod 12:39), in the seven-day Passover season's enacted holiness-demand (no leaven in any dwelling), and in the New Testament's apostolic extension of the leaven-purge metaphor to the Christian community's call to live as an unleavened holy congregation.

expand to see more

Exodus 12:39 — the historical origin: the Israelites baked unleavened cakes because they were thrust out of Egypt suddenly and could not wait for the dough to rise; urgency and deliverance are baked into the bread from the first moment

Exodus 12:15–20; 13:3–10 — the covenant legislation: leaven to be utterly purged from the household for seven days; the severity of the sanction (“cut off from Israel”) reflects how seriously God treats the holiness-type

Leaven as sin-type — Matt 16:6, 11–12; 1 Cor 5:6–7: Jesus uses leaven for false teaching; Paul uses leaven for the pervasive corrupting power of tolerated sin in the church; both treatments assume the established Passover typology

First Corinthians 5:7–8 — the apostolic application: since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, the seven-day matzot-festival of holiness is now the permanent character of the Christian community; purge out the leavened man; feast with unleavened sincerity and truth

Lord's Supper connection — Luke 22:7–20: the bread Jesus took at the Last Supper was the Passover unleavened bread; matzot is the original substance of the Supper's bread element, carrying the full weight of the Passover typology into every Christian observance of it

Usage

"First Corinthians 5:7–8 makes the matzot typology the foundation of Paul's church-discipline argument: the incestuous man must be removed (“purge out the old leaven”) precisely because the church is an unleavened community for whom the Passover Lamb has been sacrificed. Church discipline is not a harsh optional extra; it is the matzot-logic applied to the living congregation. A church that tolerates visible unrepentant sin is a leavened Passover feast — an internal contradiction."

"The urgency baked into matzot — the bread of hasty departure, eaten with sandals on and staff in hand (Exod 12:11) — speaks to the Christian life's pilgrim character. The redeemed do not settle into Egypt; they eat in haste, dressed for departure, as those who belong to another country. The matzot-eating discipline of the Passover season is an annual enacted reminder that the church is always on the move, not at home in the present age."

"The leaven/matzot contrast of 1 Corinthians 5:8 — “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” versus “the leaven of malice and wickedness” — defines the texture of authentic Christian community. Sincerity (eilikrinēia, purity tested by sunlight) and truth (alētheia, unhiddenness, reality) are the positive unleavened qualities that matzot represents in the moral life of the assembly. These are not natural virtues; they are the fruit of a community whose Passover Lamb has been slain and whose leaven has been purged."
